sections.3.0:
Before we go further into Bitcoin, it's worth understanding how money got to where it is today. This chapter traces that path — from direct trade between people, all the way to the card or app you use now.

Activity: before reading on, try the Barter Game with your group — attempt to trade for something you actually want using only objects you brought today, no money allowed. Notice how hard it gets.

As you play the Barter Game, pay close attention to the exact moment things get frustrating, and to what specifically causes that frustration. It's rarely that nobody wants what you have — it's usually that the person who wants what you have doesn't have what you want, or that what you have can't be split into a size that matches the trade you're trying to make. Hold onto that specific feeling. Every solution covered in this chapter — coins, paper money, cards — exists because someone, at some point in history, got frustrated in exactly that same way and tried to build something better.
sections.3.1:
The earliest form of trade was barter — swapping one useful thing directly for another. A farmer with extra maize might trade it for a fisherman's catch.

Barter works fine in small, simple communities. But it runs into a specific, repeated problem: you need what's called a 'double coincidence of wants.' Not only do you need to find someone who has what you want, they also need to want what you have, at the same time. A fisherman who wants shoes but not maize is a dead end — even if the shoemaker desperately wants fish.

As trade grew beyond small villages, this limitation became a real bottleneck. Humans needed something else.

It's worth noticing how quickly this problem compounds as an economy grows. In a village of ten people, each person roughly knows what everyone else has and wants, so barter is merely inconvenient. In a town of ten thousand people trading across dozens of different goods and services, the odds of any two people having a perfect double coincidence of wants at the same moment become vanishingly small. Historically, larger and more specialized economies didn't just find barter inconvenient — they found it genuinely impossible to run at scale. This is why every society that grew large enough eventually converged on some form of money, independently, in different parts of the world, without copying each other. That's a strong signal that money isn't an arbitrary invention — it's closer to a mathematical necessity of large-scale trade.
sections.3.1.1:
Early societies experimented with all kinds of objects to solve the double-coincidence problem — cattle, grain, shells, salt (the origin of the word 'salary'). Each solved the barter problem partially, but came with real weaknesses.

Cattle don't divide into small units. Grain rots. Shells can sometimes be found too easily nearby, undermining their scarcity. Every one of these early moneys was a tradeoff — good at some of the properties of sound money, weak at others.

The word 'salary' is worth dwelling on for a moment, because it's a small piece of linguistic evidence for something huge: Roman soldiers were historically paid partly in salt, valuable at the time for preserving food long before refrigeration existed. That single word surviving into modern English, attached to every payslip today, is a reminder that 'what counts as money' has shifted dramatically over just a few thousand years — and that the shift is still ongoing. It's easy to assume the money you grew up using is simply 'real' money and everything before it was primitive. A more accurate way to think about it: every generation uses whatever form of money best solves that era's specific version of the coordination problem, given the technology available at the time. Salt made sense before refrigeration. Coins made sense once metalworking was reliable. The next few sections trace exactly how each new solution replaced the one before it, and why.
sections.3.1.2:
Metal coinage was a major leap forward. Metals like gold and silver were durable, divisible into smaller units, and relatively scarce — solving several of barter's problems at once.

Standardized coinage, stamped by an authority to guarantee weight and purity, made trade dramatically easier across longer distances and between strangers who'd never met. Paper money came later, originally as a receipt: a promise that the paper could be redeemed for a fixed amount of gold or silver held safely elsewhere. That backing is the key detail to hold onto for later chapters.

The stamp on a coin deserves more attention than it usually gets, because it represents something genuinely new: institutional trust replacing personal trust. Before standardized coinage, if you handed someone an unmarked lump of gold, they'd reasonably want to verify its weight and purity themselves — weighing it, testing it, perhaps biting it. A stamped coin from a recognized authority let two total strangers skip that entire verification step, because both trusted the same third party's guarantee. This is a pattern you'll see recur throughout this Diploma in different forms: nearly every advance in money involves finding a new way to let strangers trust each other without having to personally verify everything themselves. Paper receipts for gold did the same job one layer further removed — you trusted the bank's promise rather than needing to carry, weigh, and verify the metal itself. Bitcoin, when you reach Chapter 6, solves this exact same underlying problem in an entirely different way — not through a trusted stamp or a trusted bank, but through a system where anyone can verify everything themselves, for free, without needing to trust any single authority at all.
sections.3.1.3:
For a long time, paper money was 'sound' — meaning it was directly backed by, and redeemable for, a scarce physical asset like gold. A banknote wasn't wealth itself; it was a claim on real wealth held in a vault.

Over the 20th century, most countries gradually severed that link. Money stopped being redeemable for anything physical and became backed only by government decree and public trust. We'll unpack exactly how and why that shift happened, and what it changed, in Chapter 4.

It's worth being precise about what actually changed when that link was severed, because the difference is easy to understate. Before the link was cut, if a government wanted to create more money, it was constrained by how much gold it actually held — creating money it couldn't back would eventually be exposed the moment enough people tried to redeem their notes at once. After the link was cut, that physical constraint disappeared entirely. A government (through its central bank) could, in principle, create new money limited only by policy choices, not by any physical scarcity. This is not automatically a disaster — there are real arguments on both sides that Chapter 4 will lay out fairly — but it is an enormous structural change, and it happened within living memory, not in some distant historical past. Many people alive today were born into a fully 'unsound,' un-backed monetary system without ever being told that a different kind of system existed for most of recorded history.
sections.3.1.4:
The most recent shift has been from physical paper and coins to plastic cards and, increasingly, numbers on a phone screen. For most people today, 'money' is barely physical at all — it's an entry in a bank's database that updates when you tap a card.

This convenience came with a tradeoff worth sitting with: your money's existence now depends entirely on a bank's systems, records, and permission. If your account is frozen or the system goes down, so does your access to your own money.

This tradeoff is easy to overlook precisely because the convenience is so large and so constant, while the risk is invisible until the exact moment it isn't. Consider what actually has to go right for you to buy groceries with a card: the bank's servers need to be online, your specific account needs to be in good standing according to that bank's own rules, the payment network connecting your bank to the shop's bank needs to be functioning, and nobody along that chain needs to have flagged your transaction as suspicious. Under normal circumstances, all of that happens invisibly, in under a second. But every one of those links is also a point where your access to your own money depends on someone else's system working correctly and someone else's permission being granted. This isn't necessarily an argument against using cards or banks day to day — it's simply naming a real dependency that most people carry without ever consciously choosing it. Chapter 7 will show you an entirely different model of holding money, where that dependency doesn't exist in the same way — along with the very different responsibilities that model asks of you instead.
sections.3.2:
Digital currency — money that exists only as data — isn't new. Banks have run on digital ledgers for decades. What's newer is the idea of digital money that doesn't depend on any single company or government to issue or control it.

That's the gap Bitcoin was built to fill, and it's exactly where this Diploma is headed next. Before we get there, though, we need to understand the system Bitcoin was responding to — fiat money — which is where Chapter 4 begins.

It's worth being precise about the actual innovation here, because it's subtle and easy to miss. Digital bank money and Bitcoin can look superficially similar — both are just numbers in a database somewhere, and neither one is physical. But the ownership and control structure underneath them is completely different. With digital bank money, a specific institution — your bank — is the sole authority that maintains the official record of your balance, and updating that record requires their systems and their permission. With the kind of digital money this Diploma is about to introduce, no single institution holds that authority; instead, thousands of independent participants around the world each maintain an identical copy of the same record and have to agree with each other before anything changes. That difference — one trusted record-keeper versus thousands of independent ones that must agree — turns out to be the single most important idea in this entire course, and Chapter 6 will show you exactly how it's technically possible to pull off.
sections.4.0:
In the last chapter we saw money slowly disconnect from any physical, scarce backing. This chapter asks the question directly: what is fiat money, and who actually controls it?

'Fiat' comes from Latin, roughly meaning 'let it be done' — a decree. Fiat money has value because a government declares it legal tender, not because it's backed by anything scarce.

That Latin root is worth sitting with, because it tells you something honest about how this form of money actually derives its value, in a way the everyday word 'money' doesn't. Nobody needs to declare that gold is valuable — people wanted it long before any government existed to make that declaration, because it's rare, durable, and useful. Fiat money works differently and, in a sense, more fragile: a rand note has essentially no value as a physical object (it's a small piece of cotton-paper with ink on it), and its worth rests entirely on a chain of trust — trust that the government will keep enforcing it as legal tender, trust that shops will keep accepting it, trust that the central bank won't create so much of it that it becomes worthless. This isn't stated to alarm you; fiat systems have worked reasonably well for long stretches in many countries. But understanding that the value is a trust-based agreement, not an inherent physical property, is the foundation for everything else in this chapter.
sections.4.1:
Most of the world moved to fully fiat currency systems within living memory — the US formally ended the dollar's convertibility to gold in 1971, and other countries followed similar paths around the same period.

This wasn't a small technical detail. It changed what money fundamentally was, from a claim on a scarce physical asset to a claim on nothing but continued public trust in the issuing government and central bank.

It's worth noting how recent and how deliberate this change actually was, because it's often taught as though it were an inevitable, gradual evolution rather than a specific set of policy decisions made by specific people at a specific moment. The 1971 decision in the United States, often referred to as the 'Nixon Shock,' was announced as a temporary measure to address a specific economic crisis at the time. It was never formally reversed. Other countries, whose currencies were pegged to the US dollar rather than directly to gold, found themselves pulled into the same fully fiat system as a consequence, whether or not their own governments had independently chosen it. Understanding this history matters because it reframes the fiat system not as a permanent, natural feature of how money must work, but as one particular arrangement, adopted within the lifetime of people still alive today, that could in principle be different.
sections.4.2:
A fiat system rests on a small number of institutions — usually a central bank and government treasury — having the authority to create new money. Understanding how that authority works, and how it interacts with the banks you use every day, is essential to understanding modern economics.

It helps to picture this as a layered system rather than a single flat one. At the top sits the central bank, which has the unique legal authority to create the base currency and set the rules commercial banks must follow. Below that sit the commercial banks you actually interact with day to day — the ones with branches and apps — which don't create the base currency themselves but do create most of the money that actually circulates, through the lending process the next few sections unpack. Below that sit ordinary users, who can earn, save, borrow, and spend that money, but who have no ability to create it. Each layer operates under real constraints, but the constraints get tighter the further down the layers you go — which is exactly the structural observation that later sections in this chapter build on when discussing who benefits most from the system's design.
sections.4.2.1:
In a fiat system, the money supply isn't fixed by anything in nature — it's set by policy decisions. A central bank can decide to create more currency, adjust interest rates, or change how much banks are required to hold in reserve.

These aren't neutral technical dials. Every one of these decisions redistributes value across society in ways that aren't always visible at the time they're made.

Take interest rates as one concrete example of how a seemingly technical dial has very real, very personal consequences. When a central bank lowers interest rates, borrowing becomes cheaper — which tends to help anyone taking out a loan for a house, a business, or a car, and tends to push up the prices of assets like property and shares, benefiting people who already own them. At the same time, lower interest rates typically mean lower returns for anyone simply keeping savings in a bank account, which tends to hurt people relying on interest income, often older or more conservative savers. Neither effect is announced as 'this decision helps borrowers and asset owners at the expense of savers' — it's usually framed in neutral macroeconomic language about stimulating growth or controlling inflation. Both framings can be true simultaneously. Learning to see the real winners and losers behind seemingly neutral monetary policy language is one of the most practically useful skills this Diploma can give you.
sections.4.2.2:
Most money in a fiat system isn't physical cash at all — it's created through lending. Under fractional reserve banking, a bank is only required to hold a fraction of its deposits in reserve, and can lend out the rest. That lent money gets deposited elsewhere, and a fraction of it gets lent out again — a chain that effectively multiplies the original deposit many times over across the banking system.

Activity: work through the Fractional Reserve Banking activity with your group — modeling this chain with a small starting deposit shows just how much new money this process creates from a single original deposit.

As you work through the activity, pay attention to a detail that surprises most people the first time they really see it: at no point in this chain does any single bank do anything that looks unusual or suspicious. Each bank is simply following an entirely normal, legal lending process — taking in deposits, keeping a required fraction in reserve, and lending out the rest to a customer who needs a loan. Yet the cumulative effect of many banks each doing this ordinary thing, one after another, is that the total amount of money circulating in the economy grows substantially beyond the original deposit — often several times over, depending on the reserve requirement. This is worth understanding precisely because it means most of the 'money' in a modern economy isn't created by a government printing press at all, in the way people often imagine — it's created, almost invisibly, through the ordinary daily lending decisions of commercial banks operating within rules set by the central bank.
sections.4.2.3:
The institutions with authority over the fiat system — central banks, commercial banks, and the governments that oversee them — sit in a structurally different position from everyone else who uses that money. They can create it; the rest of us can only earn, save, or borrow it.

This isn't a conspiracy claim, it's a structural observation worth thinking through carefully: whoever can create money first gets to spend it before its expansion affects prices — an advantage economists call the Cantillon effect. We'll return to who benefits, and who bears the cost, in Chapter 5.

The Cantillon effect is worth working through with a concrete, simplified example rather than just the definition, because the timing is the entire point. Imagine new money is created and lent to a large institution first. That institution spends it — say, buying property — while prices in the economy are still at their old, pre-expansion levels, so their money goes further. As that spending ripples outward through the economy, more people have more money to spend, and demand rises, and prices gradually rise in response. By the time that new money has fully circulated and reached an ordinary worker's wage increase, prices across the economy have already risen to reflect the larger money supply — meaning that worker's higher wage buys roughly the same as their old, lower wage did before. The institution that received the new money first benefited from the old prices; the person who received it last only ever experienced the new, higher prices. Nobody involved needs to have acted maliciously for this pattern to play out — it's simply a structural consequence of new money entering an economy at one specific point rather than appearing equally in everyone's pocket simultaneously.
sections.4.3:
Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) are a proposed next step for fiat money — a digital form of a national currency, issued and controlled directly by a central bank, rather than existing as commercial bank deposits as most digital money does today.

Several countries are actively piloting or researching CBDCs. We'll examine the tradeoffs — for privacy, for government oversight of transactions, for financial inclusion — in much more depth in Chapter 10, once you've got the full picture of fiat money, Bitcoin, and the differences between them.

It's worth previewing why CBDCs generate such strong reactions on both sides, even at this early stage of the Diploma, because it connects directly to the layered-authority picture from earlier in this chapter. Right now, when you hold money in a commercial bank account, there are technically two layers between you and the central bank — your bank's own systems sit in between. A CBDC held directly with the central bank would remove that middle layer entirely, meaning the institution with the ultimate authority to create money would also, for the first time, potentially have a direct, real-time technical relationship with every individual holder of that money. Supporters point to real efficiency gains and the possibility of reaching people who currently have no bank account at all. Critics point out that removing the middle layer also removes a layer of practical separation between an individual and the state's monetary authority — separation that today gives ordinary commercial disputes, technical glitches, and even normal banking competition a chance to soften the relationship between a citizen and centralized monetary power. Chapter 10 gives both sides of this a fair, full hearing once you have the complete toolkit to evaluate it properly.
